title: Why every section is plain Blade
author: Marcus Bell
imageAlt: A stack of plain white index cards held by a brass binder clip on an oak desk
excerpt: We could have stored pages in a database and rendered them from JSON. We chose files you can open in your editor, and it has paid for itself every week since.
content:
The first version of Starter kept pages in a database. Every section was a row, every field a JSON blob, and a renderer stitched them together on each request. It demoed well. It also meant that the moment a developer wanted to change a section, they had to leave their editor, open ours, and work through a form that knew less about HTML than they did.

We threw it out in the spring of 2025. Since then, every section in Starter is an ordinary anonymous Blade component with a small YAML file beside it. The page you edit on the canvas is a file in resources/views/pages. The canvas reads it, and when you publish, it writes it back.

What a section actually is

A section is two files. The Blade file declares its props with defaults, and renders them. The YAML file names the same props, says what kind of field each one is, and repeats the defaults. That is the whole contract.

@props(['heading' => 'Plans that grow with you'])
<h2 class="text-h2">{{ $heading }}</h2>

Starter does not annotate anything. It reads the YAML to build the inspector, and it reads the Blade to find where each field is echoed, so clicking the heading on the canvas puts a caret in the right place. If you write a new section by hand and give it a YAML file, it shows up in the Add Section picker on the next page load.

Why files won

Three things decided it for us, and none of them were about performance.

  • Review. A content change is a diff. When a marketer changes a headline, the pull request shows one attribute on one line. When a developer changes the layout of the pricing table, it shows exactly that. Nobody has to trust a dashboard’s history view.
  • Removal. If you uninstall Starter tomorrow, your site keeps serving. The runtime is one service provider that lives in your app, and it has no dependency on the editor. We think a tool that holds your pages hostage is a tool you should not adopt.
  • Everything else you already use. Blade components can call other components, read config, use @php blocks and loops. Tailwind sees the classes. Your formatter formats them. Your deploy deploys them. We did not have to build a single one of those things.

The cost

Files are harder for us than rows. The writer that turns an edit back into a page file has to change one attribute and leave every other byte alone, including your comments and your blank lines. It took Owen most of last winter to make that true across all forty templates we test against, and the test that guards it still runs on every commit: install a template, write every page back without changes, and fail if a single byte moved.

The other cost is that some things a database makes easy, like full-text search across pages, are slower to build. We decided that was a fine trade for a product whose job is a marketing site of a few dozen pages.

What it means for your team

In practice, the split is clean. Developers own the sections: their markup, their props, which fields exist. Editors own the values: the words, the images, the order of sections on a page. Neither waits on the other, and both of their changes land in the same repository.

If you have a section library already, the fastest way to try this is to add a YAML file next to one component you like and open the page in Starter. You will see its fields in the inspector in about the time it took to read this paragraph.

title: Your default copy is the design
author: Elena Ruiz
imageAlt: Five sharpened wooden pencils lying side by side on a folded sheet of cream paper
excerpt: The words a section ships with are what every visitor sees until someone edits them. So we write them the way the product would, not the way a template would.
content:
When we review a new section, the first thing we read is not the markup. It is the default values in its YAML file. Those strings are what a team sees the moment they add the section to a page, and for a surprising number of sites, they are what goes live.

That makes defaults a design decision, not a placeholder to be filled in later. A section that ships with placeholder Latin or “Feature one” teaches nothing about how it should be used. A section that ships with a specific headline, a real-looking price and a testimonial with a full name shows exactly how much text each slot was drawn for.

Write for one invented product

Every section in the library is written for one product with a job. The pricing section sells a tool with three plans at $0, $29 and $79. The FAQ answers questions somebody would actually ask before paying. When the copy is about something, the layout is tested against real lengths: a plan description that wraps to two lines, a question that runs long, a name with a hyphen.

We keep a few rules on the wall:

  • Headlines under eight words, in sentence case, with no exclamation marks.
  • Numbers are specific. “11 days” and “4.9 from 312 reviews” read as true; “10x” and “thousands of happy customers” read as filler.
  • Buttons say what happens next: “Start free”, “See pricing”, “Book a demo”. Never “Submit” and never “Learn more”.
  • People get a full name, a role and a company. A quote without a name is just an opinion.

Length is part of the layout

A three-column feature grid is drawn for three short titles and three single sentences. If one description runs to four lines, the row stops lining up and the section looks broken, even though nothing is wrong with the code. So when we write defaults, we write them to the length the layout was designed for, and the field’s help text says so.

We check this at three widths before a section ships: a phone at 390 pixels, a tablet at 768 and a laptop at 1280. A headline that sits on two lines at 1280 and breaks into five at 390 usually means the default is too long, not that the type is too big. Shortening the copy fixes it everywhere; shrinking the type only moves the problem.

The same goes for images. Each image field names the aspect it was drawn for. A 21:9 slot that receives a square photo will crop it, and the crop will be wherever the browser decides. Saying “a wide 21:9 crop works best” in the field description saves a round of confused messages to support.

Defaults travel

Because a section’s defaults live in its own files, they travel with it. When you add a testimonial wall to a new page, it arrives complete, with six quotes of different lengths, so you can see how the masonry behaves before you write your own. Bind it to your testimonials collection and the rows switch over; unbind it and the defaults come back.

The test we apply before a section ships is simple. If a visitor landed on a page made only of default values, would it read like a real company’s site? If the answer is no, the section is not finished, however good the markup is.

title: The ticket we stopped filing
author: Dana Whitfield
imageAlt: An empty black wire inbox tray on a white desk next to a mug and a potted plant
excerpt: Before Starter, two of us ran a small agency. A third of our tickets were someone asking us to change a sentence. This is the story of how that number went to zero.
content:
Marcus and I ran a five-person web agency in Columbus for six years. We built marketing sites for software companies, clinics, a few restaurants, and one very particular climbing gym. Every site was Laravel, every site had a handful of Blade components we had written a dozen times before, and every site generated the same kind of ticket after launch.

“Can you change the headline on the pricing page?” “We need to swap the photo in the second section.” “Our new head of sales wants the button to say Book a demo.”

In our last full year, 34% of the tickets we closed were copy changes. Each one took a developer about twenty minutes once you counted the context switch, the branch, the review and the deploy. That is roughly 300 hours a year of skilled people changing words.

What we tried first

We tried a headless CMS. The clients could edit text, but every new section needed a schema in one place and a component in another, and the two drifted. We tried a hosted page builder for the marketing pages and Laravel for everything else. The clients liked it until the two halves of their site looked like two companies.

What we wanted was simple to describe: let the client edit the words and images directly on the page they are looking at, and have that edit land in the same Blade files we already wrote. No second system to keep in sync.

The rule that made it work

The idea that turned into Starter was a rule, not a feature. Every visible string, link, image and list in a section is a field, and every field has a default. If a client would want to change it, it is editable. If it is editable, it is in the YAML.

Once that was true, the copy tickets stopped. Not slowed down: stopped. Clients opened the page, clicked the headline, typed, and pressed Publish. We saw the change in the next pull request like everyone else.

What the developers got back

The part I did not expect was how much the developers liked it. Nobody enjoys changing “Get started” to “Start free” for the third time in a month. With copy out of the queue, the tickets that were left were the interesting ones: a new section, a faster page, an integration.

Where the time went instead

In the year after we moved our own clients onto the first version, our copy-change tickets went from 34% of the queue to under 2%, and the ones that remained were usually a request for a section that did not exist yet. We used the hours on two things: faster sites, and a better section library. Both of those became Starter.

That is still the whole pitch, really. Starter is not trying to replace your developers or your stack. It is trying to make sure the people who write the words never have to wait on the people who write the code, and the other way around.

title: How page changes became instant
author: Owen Park
imageAlt: A white paper airplane resting on a sunlit concrete ledge against a blue sky
excerpt: Every site made with Starter now swaps pages in place: links are fetched on intent and the main content changes without a reload. Here is how it works, and what it asked of sections.
content:
A marketing site is small. Most have fewer than thirty pages, and most visitors look at three of them. That makes it a good candidate for a trick that would be reckless on a large app: fetch the next page before the visitor asks for it, and swap it in without a full load.

Since 2.13, every Starter site does this out of the box. Hovering a link for 80 milliseconds, focusing it, or touching it fetches the page into memory. The click replaces the page’s <main> with the new one, keeps the header and footer where they are, and updates the title, the history and the scroll position. On our own site, the median click-to-paint went from 410 ms to 38 ms.

What we did not build

We did not build a client-side router, and we did not turn sites into single-page apps. Every page is still a complete HTML document that the server renders. If the script is blocked, the network is slow, or the link goes somewhere unusual, the browser loads the page the ordinary way. The floor is a normal website.

The runtime is one small file. It ignores other origins, downloads, mailto: and tel: links, anything with target="_blank", and clicks with a modifier key. A link can opt out with a single attribute, which we use for the sign-in link into the app.

What it asked of sections

The hard part was not the swap. It was every script that assumed it would only run once.

A pricing toggle that binds its click handler on page load works on the page you land on and nowhere else. A scroll reveal that sets up its observer on load leaves every later page’s content invisible. We found eleven of these across the section library the first afternoon we turned it on.

The fix was a convention. Anything that touches page content is a function that takes a root element and is called twice: once on load, and again whenever a new page arrives.

function setUp(root) {
    reveals(root);
    pricingToggle(root);
}
setUp(document);
document.addEventListener('site:navigated', (e) => setUp(e.detail.main));

Sections that carry their own small script write it as a self-contained function that checks whether it has already run on its element. The runtime re-creates those scripts when their page arrives, so they keep working.

Keeping it fast

Fetching ahead only pays if pages are light enough to be worth fetching. So the rest of the usual advice still applies: images below the fold load lazily, every image has a width and a height so nothing jumps after a swap, and the hero image is the only one fetched eagerly.

We also cap what we fetch. The navigation’s links are fetched once the page is idle; everything else waits for intent. On a phone with data saver on, nothing is fetched ahead at all.

Try it

If your site was installed before 2.13, run the update and the switch is already on in the layout. Click between two pages with the network panel open and you will see one request on hover and nothing on click. That nothing is the whole feature.

title: What 212 pricing pages taught us
author: Sam Okada
imageAlt: Three white ceramic bowls of increasing size on a sage green linen cloth
excerpt: Over the summer we read the pricing pages of 212 software companies that publish with Starter. Seven patterns separated the pages that convert from the ones that confuse.
content:
Pricing pages are the most edited pages on Starter sites. Teams change a plan name, add a feature line, move a price, and change it back two weeks later. Over the summer we read 212 of them, with permission, alongside each company’s trial sign-up rate. Here is what held up.

1. Three plans, one of them obvious

Pages with three plans and one clearly highlighted had the highest sign-up rate. Four plans did a little worse; five did noticeably worse. The highlight matters less for its color than for its position: the middle plan, lifted a few pixels and outlined, was the one most often chosen.

2. The yearly switch shows the saving in dollars

“Save 17%” asks the visitor to do arithmetic. “$290 a year, two months free” does not. The pages that showed the yearly price as a real number, with the monthly equivalent in small type underneath, kept more visitors on the yearly option.

3. Every plan says who it is for

A one-line description under each plan name, written as a person rather than a feature list, outperformed pages without one. “Real client work: your own domains, more sites, and someone to answer the phone” tells an agency which plan it is. “Advanced features” tells nobody anything.

4. The feature list is short, and the table is optional

The plan cards that converted best listed five lines or fewer, starting with “Everything in Free”. The full comparison sat below, in a table of no more than eight rows, for the visitors who wanted it. Pages that put a forty-row table first lost people before they reached a button.

5. The FAQ answers the money questions

The best pricing FAQs answered four things: can I try it first, what happens when I upgrade or downgrade, can I leave with my data, and what support do I get. Pages that answered these in two sentences each saw fewer “quick question” emails to sales.

6. One button label per plan

Buttons that named the plan (“Upgrade to Pro”) did better than ones that repeated “Get started” three times. It is a small thing, but it confirms the choice at the moment of making it.

7. A way out for the big customer

Almost every page that sold to larger teams had a quiet line under the plans for anyone who needed more: a security review, an invoice instead of a card, a contract. A text link to talk to sales was enough. It did not need its own plan.

What did not matter

A few things we expected to matter did not show up in the numbers at all: whether prices sat above or below the plan name, whether the page used cards or columns, and whether there was a money-back guarantee badge. Visitors read the plan, the price and the first three lines of the list. Everything else was decoration.

Using this on your own page

Starter’s pricing section already follows most of these: three plans from a collection, one marked as featured, a yearly switch that rewrites the prices, and a note line under each. If you change only one thing this week, rewrite the description under each plan so it names a kind of customer. It is the cheapest change on the list and one of the most effective.

title: What 1,600 support emails taught us
author: Nia Thompson
imageAlt: Reading glasses resting on an open notebook beside a cup of black coffee
excerpt: I read every message that reaches support. After 1,600 of them this year, a handful of questions account for most of the inbox, and most of them were about the editor, not the code.
content:
Support at Starter is me, most days, with Sam covering the phone line on Business accounts. I read every message that comes in, and since January that has been 1,612 of them. About a fifth are billing questions. The rest are about using the product, and a surprising share of those were not about code at all.

“Where did my change go?”

The most common question, by a distance, came from editors who had changed a page and could not see it on the live site. The answer was almost always the same: the change was saved as a draft and had not been published yet.

We had a publish button. It just did not say how many unpublished changes were waiting. In 2.11 we added a small dot to the button and a list of changed pages inside it. That question went from about thirty a month to four.

“Why can’t I edit this?”

The second most common: an editor clicks a list of logos or testimonials on the canvas and gets no caret. Those lists are bound to a collection, so their rows are edited in one place and every section that shows them follows. That is the right behavior, but nothing on the canvas said so.

Now a bound list is one target. Clicking it opens a small card beside it with the rows, and a link to the full table. Nobody has asked this question since August.

“Can I undo that?”

Deleting a section used to ask for confirmation. People clicked through the dialog without reading it and then wrote to us. We removed the dialog and added an Undo button to the message that appears afterward. Fewer clicks, fewer mistakes, fewer emails.

What developers ask

Developer questions cluster around three things: how to make a new field show up in the inspector (add it to the YAML and the props, with the same default), how to bind a list to a collection (a source line in the YAML), and how to keep a section’s script working after a page swap. The documentation now opens with all three.

“Will this break my site?”

A quieter question, but an important one, came from developers about to try Starter on an existing app. They wanted to know what it would touch. The honest answer is: the folder your site lives in, one service provider, and nothing else. We now say that on the install page in one sentence, and the question has mostly gone away. When it does come in, I send the same reply: try it on a branch, and delete the branch if you do not like it.

How we use the inbox

Every Friday, I tag the week’s messages by what they were really about, and the five most common tags go into the planning meeting on Monday. It is not sophisticated. It is the most reliable source of product decisions we have, and it costs one afternoon a week.

If you write to us, you will get a reply from a person within one business day, and there is a decent chance your question changes the product.
